Fat graft survival

One rat experiment found greater graft weight and volume retention at 56 days when polychromatic light was applied both before and after transfer. Vascularity and adipocyte-viability markers increased, while several tissue-damage measures decreased.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One rat experiment found greater graft weight and volume retention at 56 days when polychromatic light was applied both before and after transfer. Vascularity and adipocyte-viability markers increased, while several tissue-damage measures decreased.

Summary of the Evidence

One publication reports a four-group experiment in 24 rats, six per group, comparing no light, pre-transfer light, post-transfer light, and both. The study tested a broad-spectrum lamp around fat grafting and did not report duplicate publications. No human trial or separate cell-culture study of PBM for fat-graft survival was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study was found testing whether PBM improves fat retention or contour after human fat transfer. The animal endpoints of retained weight, volume, and graft histology are relevant to graft survival but do not establish patient-visible results or long-term stability.

Animal evidence

At 56 days, the group treated both before and after transfer retained significantly more graft weight and volume than the other groups. Histology showed more vascularization and viable adipocytes, with less necrosis, fibrosis, inflammation, and cyst formation. Perilipin, CD31, and VEGF staining was higher, while Ki67 staining was lower. The findings favor the combined timing protocol in this experiment; they do not show that either the pre- or post-transfer exposure alone produced the same effect (Sert et al. 2022).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No stand-alone cell-culture or ex-vivo PBM study directly evaluating fat-graft retention was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The authors used polychromatic light spanning 600–1200 nm, from visible red light through near-infrared. The reported fluence was 31.2 J/cm², each exposure lasted 720 seconds, and the schedule included seven sessions over seven days. Light was applied to the recipient site before and after graft transfer in the best-performing group. The report did not provide a full power or irradiance profile for the broad-spectrum source, and it did not compare individual wavelengths or doses.

Interpretation

The combined pre- and post-transfer protocol improved measured graft retention and several tissue-quality outcomes in this rat model. This is a favorable result for one small experiment, not evidence that PBM improves long-term volume retention after human fat grafting.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for graft retention and tissue viability in rats
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A single small rat experiment found greater retained graft weight and volume when broad-spectrum light was applied both before and after fat transfer, alongside better vascular and adipocyte measures. The result has not been replicated in people or another animal cohort. Independent studies with longer volume follow-up and clear dose reporting would be needed for a stronger conclusion.
